hints: Look back at Table 1.1 and write down the exact genotype of each parent - Golden Dawn and Tondo di Piacenza. What allele must each parent give to every gamete?
Think about what happens when a dominant allele meets a recessive allele in the F1. Which colour allele and which shape allele will be expressed?
walkthrough:
Work Out The F1 Genotype From The Parents**
Golden Dawn is $AAbb$ so it can only make $Ab$ gametes. Tondo di Piacenza is $aaBB$ so it can only make $aB$ gametes. Put them together at fertilisation and every F1 plant must be $AaBb$ - heterozygous at both genes.

Translate Genotype Into Phenotype And Spot The Surprise**
You are told $A$ gives yellow and $B$ gives round when present, even in one copy. So $AaBb$ is yellow and round. The gardener grew Golden Dawn (yellow long) and Tondo (green round) side by side. Neither parent is yellow and round, so a completely new combination appearing in all the F1 seeds would be unexpected.
Final answer: F1 fruits are yellow and round (genotype AaBb). This was unexpected as fruits do not resemble either parent / resemble Floridor variety.

hints: Start from the F1 genotype you found in (a)(i). Because the two genes are on different chromosomes, how many different gamete combinations can an AaBb plant make?
Remember to place those four gamete types along the top and side of Fig. 1.1 before filling any inner squares.
When filling the square, focus first on getting genotypes right by combining row and column alleles, then ask for each box whether A and B are present.
For the final ratio, count how many of the 16 boxes fall into each phenotype class and keep them in the classic dihybrid order.
walkthrough:
Get The Four F1 Gametes Right**
The cross is $AaBb$ x $AaBb$. Because genes $A/a$ and $B/b$ are on different chromosomes they assort independently in meiosis. Each parent makes four gamete types in equal numbers: $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$. Put these as row and column headings in Fig. 1.1.

Fill The Punnett Square Systematically**
Join each row gamete with each column gamete. For example $AB$ x $ab$ gives $AaBb$, $Ab$ x $Ab$ gives $AAbb$, $aB$ x $aB$ gives $aaBB$, $ab$ x $ab$ gives $aabb$. Complete all 16 boxes carefully - one slip changes the count.

Convert Genotypes To Phenotypes And Ratio**
Any genotype with $A-$ is yellow, $aa$ is green. Any with $B-$ is round, $bb$ is long. Counting gives 9 yellow round ($AABB$, $AABb$, $AaBB$, $AaBb$), 3 yellow long ($AAbb$, $Aabb$), 3 green round ($aaBB$, $aaBb$), 1 green long ($aabb$). So ratio is 9 yellow round : 3 yellow long : 3 green round : 1 green long.
Final answer: F1 gametes: $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$. F2 genotypes give 9 $A-B-$ yellow round : 3 $A-bb$ yellow long : 3 $aaB-$ green round : 1 $aabb$ green long.

hints: Work out the chromosome number of the triploid from the parents given - diploid 2n = 22 crossed with tetraploid 4n = 44. Is the result even or odd?
Recall what must happen to homologous chromosomes at the start of meiosis for gametes to form normally.
Link failure of that meiotic event to fertilisation and seed formation - seeds are formed when male and female gametes fuse.
walkthrough:
Why Three Sets Is A Problem**
Diploid gives n = 11, tetraploid gives 2n = 22, so triploid is 3n = 33. That is an odd number, meaning three copies of each homologous chromosome in every cell.

What Fails In Meiosis**
For normal meiosis, homologous chromosomes must pair up to form bivalents by synapsis in prophase I, then separate evenly. With three copies, pairing cannot be even - you get unpaired chromosomes or uneven segregation. Meiosis is disrupted and cannot produce balanced haploid nuclei.

From No Gametes To No Seeds**
Without successful meiosis, functional male and female gametes, pollen and ovules, are not formed. You are told seeds are the structures formed when male and female gametes fuse at fertilisation. No gametes means no fertilisation, so fruits develop but are sterile and seedless.

Final answer: Triploid has 33 chromosomes / odd number / three copies of each homologue, so chromosomes cannot all pair up / form bivalents in prophase I. Meiosis is disrupted so viable gametes / ovules and pollen are not formed, so no fertilisation and no seeds.

hints: Compare the two plants named - one is Citrullus lanatus with 2n = 22 and the other is Cucurbita ecuadorensis with 2n = 40. What does that tell you about successful breeding?
walkthrough:
Spot The Breeding Barrier**
Watermelon is Citrullus with 2n = 22, the resistant plant is Cucurbita with 2n = 40. They are not just different species but different genera with very different chromosome numbers. Chromosomes could not pair normally in a hybrid, so conventional crossing cannot give a fertile WMV-resistant watermelon variety.
Final answer: They are different genera / have different chromosome numbers (22 and 40) so any offspring would be sterile / breeding cannot succeed.

hints: Since normal crossing is blocked, think of the method that moves just one useful gene between unrelated organisms without needing fertilisation.
Recall the two key tools needed - one to cut out the resistance gene from donor DNA and one to carry it into watermelon cells.
walkthrough:
Choose Genetic Modification**
The answer is genetic engineering, also called genetic modification or recombinant DNA technology. This bypasses sexual reproduction and lets you move the single WMV-resistance gene across the genus barrier.

Cut And Deliver The Gene**
Use a restriction enzyme (endonuclease) to cut the resistance gene out of Cucurbita ecuadorensis DNA. Then place it into a vector such as a plasmid or use Agrobacterium tumefaciens to insert the gene into watermelon cells, which are then grown into resistant plants.

Final answer: Use genetic engineering / recombinant DNA technology. Cut WMV-resistance gene from C. ecuadorensis DNA with restriction enzyme / endonuclease and insert into watermelon cells using a vector / plasmid / Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
